principal_investigators: Marshall B. Long (Yale University) - Principal Investigator

identity.hardware: ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) chamber insert with the small coflow burner (fuel tube ~2.1-2.2 mm inner diameter inside a 25 mm air nozzle), crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers, colour and gray-scale cameras, PMTs and thin-filament pyrometry fibres

one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames surrounded by a gentle co-flowing air stream were burned on the Space Station, from very diluted near-extinction flames to very sooty ones, to give computer models clean, buoyancy-free benchmark data; the sooty flames held several times more soot than on Earth and diluted flames survived at lower fuel concentrations.
summary: CLD Flame produced benchmark data on laminar coflow diffusion flames, a fuel jet surrounded by co-flowing air, for testing chemical-kinetic and soot models at both extremes of fuel dilution. On the ISS, in the ACME insert of the Combustion Integrated Rack, a small coflow burner (about 2 mm fuel tube in a 25 mm air nozzle) burned nitrogen-diluted methane (20-100%) and ethylene (10-100%) in air on 32 test days from November 2017 to March 2021, igniting 344 flames. Cameras and pyrometry gave flame shape, lift-off height, CH* chemiluminescence, temperature, soot temperature and soot volume fraction. Preliminary results: sooty microgravity flames were taller and wider and held 5-8 times more soot than equivalent 1 g flames, and dilution limits of both fuels were extended, with lifted flames stable at lower fuel concentrations. Simulations of the ACME ethylene flames showed weaker gravity effects than in a larger burner, and highlighted errors in the predicted temperature field. For fire safety this is fundamental: microgravity flames can be sootier, more radiative and burn closer to dilution limits.

question.text: Can detailed computational models with chemical-kinetic and soot sub-models predict laminar diffusion flames at the extremes of fuel dilution: heavily sooting pure-fuel flames and very dilute flames near extinction? Earlier work, including microgravity work, showed the models fall short there. Buoyancy complicates 1 g flames (it accelerates and narrows them, shortens residence time and causes flicker), so the ISS was used to obtain momentum-dominated, buoyancy-free coflow flames with long residence times as clean benchmark cases. Objective A: characterise weak coflow methane and ethylene flames versus velocity and dilution (flame shape, lift-off height, temperature, extinction limits). Objective B: characterise sooting tendency of long-residence-time flames versus velocity and dilution (shape, gas temperature in soot-free regions, soot luminosity, soot temperature, soot volume fraction). The stated hypothesis is to supply benchmark data to validate the investigators' computational models. Motivation is terrestrial combustion (efficiency, pollutants, design tools); NASA states the work does not serve space applications.

sources.quote: Past research, including that conducted in microgravity, had revealed shortfalls in the ability to accurately model flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.

The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
Improve computational flame models with benchmark quantitative data for sooty and extremely diluted microgravity flames.

The CLD Flame research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing).

physics.text: In a coflow laminar diffusion flame, fuel (here methane or ethylene, often diluted with nitrogen) issues from a central tube into a surrounding stream of air; fuel and oxygen meet by diffusion and burn in a thin sheet roughly where they meet in stoichiometric proportion. On Earth the hot, light products are accelerated upward by buoyancy, which stretches and narrows the flame, pulls in air radially and shortens the time gas spends in the hot sooting region; the flame also flickers. In microgravity the flow is set only by the injection momentum, so flames are longer, wider and more diffuse, residence times are longer, and temperatures are lower. Longer residence time lets soot particles grow, so sooty flames carry several times more soot; more soot means more radiative loss, which cools the flame, which in turn changes soot chemistry - a strongly coupled problem that models struggle with. At the dilute extreme the flame is weak and lifts off the burner, stabilising where the local flow speed matches the propagation speed of its leading (triple-flame) edge; working with lifted flames removes heat loss to the burner rim from the problem. Without buoyancy-induced acceleration, dilute flames survive at lower fuel concentrations. Diluting the fuel with nitrogen lowers flame temperature and moves the stoichiometric surface, so dilution and velocity are the two knobs spanning weak to heavily sooting flames. Drop towers give only ~5 s, too short for soot to reach quasi-steady conditions, hence the need for ISS duration.

sources.note: Coflow diffusion-flame structure, buoyancy effects on residence time, soot-radiation coupling and lifted-flame stabilisation by edge (triple) flames are textbook combustion background.

equations.meaning: Burke-Schumann/Roper scaling for the length of a laminar jet diffusion flame. $L_f$ flame length (m); $\dot{m}_F$ mass flow rate of the fuel mixture (kg/s); $\rho D$ density times diffusivity of the gas (kg m-1 s-1, roughly temperature-independent); $S$ moles of oxidiser stream needed per mole of fuel stream (dilution changes $S$). Length depends on fuel mass flow, not separately on velocity or burner diameter, to leading order in both buoyant and non-buoyant flames; buoyancy and coflow change the prefactor and the flame width. Consistent with the SLICE finding that luminous flame length is proportional to fuel mass flow in both 1 g and microgravity, with microgravity flames longer.

sources.note: Roper (1977) laminar jet flame length correlations

sources.quote: Buoyant and nonbuoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to the mass flow rate of the fuel mixture; computed and measured nonbuoyant flames are noticeably longer than their 1g counterparts

equations.meaning: Stoichiometric mixture fraction, locating the flame sheet in mixture-fraction space. $Y_{F,1}$ fuel mass fraction in the fuel stream (lowered by N2 dilution); $Y_{O_2,2}$ = 0.233, oxygen mass fraction in air; $s$ stoichiometric oxygen-to-fuel mass ratio (4.0 for CH4, 3.43 for C2H4). Dilution raises $Z_{st}$ and lowers flame temperature and soot formation, which is how the fuel concentrations in the experimental table span sooty to near-extinction flames. Valid for a one-step, equal-diffusivity picture.

Froude number comparing jet momentum to buoyancy for exit velocity $U$ (m/s), tube diameter $d$ (m) and gravity $g$ (9.81 m/s2 on Earth); residence time $t_{res}$ (s) of gas in a flame of length $L_f$ (m). For the ACME burner ($d \approx 2$ mm, $U$ of order 10-100 cm/s) $Fr$ in 1 g is of order 0.5-50, so small slow flames are buoyancy-affected on Earth; in orbit ($g \approx 10^{-6} g_0$) they are momentum-dominated and gas lingers longer, giving more time for soot growth. Order-of-magnitude only.

sources.note: standard dimensional analysis; values are illustrative

equations.meaning: Two-colour (colour-ratio) soot pyrometry used with the calibrated colour camera, in the Wien approximation: $S_1/S_2$ signal ratio of two colour channels at effective wavelengths $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ (m); $\eta_{12}$ instrument calibration factor; $\alpha$ soot dispersion exponent (emissivity $\propto \lambda^{-\alpha}$; 0.9-1.38 assumed for microgravity soot in the SLICE analysis); $C_2$ = 0.014388 m K; $T_s$ soot temperature (K). Soot volume fraction $f_v$ (dimensionless, ppm) then follows from the absolute emission (calibrated against a thermocouple) via spectral emissivity $\varepsilon_\lambda$ over path length $L$ (m) with dimensionless extinction coefficient $K_e$. Assumes optically thin, line-of-sight data after Abel inversion; self-absorption in sooty flames biases temperature (corrections up to 22-75 K).

sources.quote: While the true soot dispersion exponent remains unknown in microgravity, a range from 0.9 to 1.38 is estimated based on literature values

with the maximum correction quantified to be 22 K for a flame with a maximum optical depth of 0.31. This correction is as much as 42 and 75 K for simulated flames with the same optical properties, structure, and a factor of two and five increase in soot volume fraction, respectively.

apparatus.text: ACME chamber insert in the CIR combustion chamber (nominally 100 L, ~83 L free volume; constant-volume tests lasting a few minutes). Small coflow burner: two concentric tubes of 2.1 mm (fuel) and 25 mm (air) inner diameter; a 2023 modelling paper gives 2.2 mm inner diameter with 0.1 mm wall. The same burner was later used by E-FIELD Flames. Gas delivery by crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers (fuel, nitrogen diluent, coflow); per test day the fuel MFC full scale was 0.1 or 0.2 slpm and the N2 MFC 0.02-0.2 slpm (nitrogen basis). Diagnostics: a pre-characterised high-definition colour camera (flame shape, lift-off, CH* concentration, flame and soot temperature by pyrometry, soot volume fraction), a gray-scale camera with an opposed collimated light source for soot by light extinction, intensified cameras for OH* and CH*, PMTs for CH*/OH* chemiluminescence, radiometers, and translating 14 micron SiC fibres for thin-filament pyrometry (TFP) of gas temperature. Tests configured by crew and commanded from NASA Glenn.

procedure.text: Each test day the crew set up the burner, fuel bottle and mass flow controllers, and tests were run from the ground. Flames were ignited in an air-filled chamber with an air coflow, fuel and air velocities typically matched; fuel concentration (N2 dilution) and velocity were varied between tests and sometimes during a test, stepping toward lower fuel concentration until extinction for the dilute-limit work. Three ISS rounds: methane, 14 days (2017-11-15 to 2018-02-22, 130 flames); ethylene, 14 days (2018-05-25 to 2018-09-14, 162 flames); 'improved coflow tests', 4 days (2021-02-10 to 2021-03-03; 2 ethylene, 2 methane; 52 flames). Total 32 test days, 344 flames. Normal-gravity comparison flames were burned at Yale, and the investigators' MC-Smooth vorticity-velocity code with sectional soot model was used to compute both. The precursor SLICE experiment (Microgravity Science Glovebox, January-March 2012) used a different burner (76 mm square duct, 5 interchangeable nozzles) to refine the test matrix; most published ISS results in the PSI publication list come from SLICE, not from these ACME test days.

relevance.text: CLD Flame is not a fire-safety experiment (NASA: no space application intended). Its relevance is fundamental: (1) in still or slow flows microgravity flames can carry several times more soot and lose more heat by radiation than the same flames on Earth, which affects smoke production (detection) and radiative heating of nearby surfaces; (2) dilute flames survived to lower fuel concentrations in microgravity, so dilution or inerting margins derived from 1 g flames may be non-conservative for gaseous fuel leaks in orbit; (3) validated soot/radiation models are a prerequisite for predictive spacecraft fire simulation. Transferability caveats: small laminar gas-jet flames in air with nitrogen-diluted fuel; no solid or liquid fuels, no oxygen enrichment or reduced pressure; extinction data are fuel-dilution limits of a burner flame, not material flammability limits.

habitat_conditions.text: All tests used air (about 21% O2) as oxidiser; chamber pressure is not stated in sources reached and is presumably near the Earth sea-level reference (101.3 kPa), but this is not documented. No enriched-oxygen or reduced-pressure cases such as the lunar habitat concept (>=30% O2 at <=70.3 kPa) were run; a ground companion study (1.0-2.7 atm, 101-274 kPa) examined only elevated pressure. Gravity: ISS microgravity only; no partial-gravity data.

earth_benefits.text: Better kinetic and soot models for diffusion flames, the flame type of most practical combustors, should improve efficiency and reduce pollutant and soot emissions, and shorten the design time and cost of furnaces and engines; understanding extinction also informs fire suppression.

sources.quote: Furthermore, improved design capability can enable reduced time and cost in the development of new furnaces and engines.

Headline result (4-8x soot, ~200 K cooler) from SLICE and ACME summaries; values must come from external sources.

gaps: No Science Documents, Reports, Presentations, Analyzed or Raw Data in PSI: only the experimental table CSV and a metadata zip. All results come from the PSI record text and external sources.
Per-test fuel and coflow velocities, lift-off heights, extinction concentrations, temperatures and soot data are not in PSI; chamber pressure is not stated anywhere reached.

Full texts of the Elsevier papers (Giassi 2016, Cao 2015, Ma 2015, Kempema 2021) were not read from the publisher (ScienceDirect blocks automated access); NASA NTRS preprints of Ma 2015 (20140017780), Cao 2015 (20150002322) and a Giassi CH* abstract/poster (20160012298) were used instead, and Crossref/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar abstracts for Dobbins 2022, Cao 2018, Kempema 2018 and 2021. Dobbins 2022 (Taylor & Francis) full text was not reachable.

The ACME CLD Flame conference papers cited by NASA for ISS results (Tinajero, Giassi, Stocker & Long, 11th US National Combustion Meeting 2019; Tinajero & Long, 12th USNCM 2021) were not found online.
Most publications listed in the PSI record are SLICE-precursor or ground studies; one DOI (10.1016/j.proci.2014.05.138) is listed twice. The PSI record does not list SLICE (PSI-106) as related.

Table data issues: the 'Fuel Bottle' column is a spreadsheet auto-fill artefact after the first row of each block ('40% CH5' ... '40% CH14', '100% C2H5' ... '100% C2H11', '50% C2H5' ... '50% C2H9', '30% C2H5', '40% CH5'); the bottles are presumably 40% CH4, 100% CH4, 100%/50%/30% C2H4. data/processed/tests.csv carries these labels in fuel_raw and leaves fuel_fraction mostly empty. 2018-02-22 (18053) lists a 100% CH4 bottle diluted to 30-40% with only a 0.02 slpm N2 MFC, which implies very low fuel flows - possible but worth checking. 2021-02-10 (21041) lists '0%-30%'.
Brief said 32 test days; confirmed (32 rows, 344 flames). The evidence.parquet chunk for the table previews only rows 1-5; other rows were read from the CSV.

Metadata zip is named 'PSI-21_metadata_PSI-97_ACME CLD Flame.zip' (refers to PSI-97); files.csv marks it not downloaded although a 16,071-byte file (listed size 15,476) is on disk. Record totalFileSize (~2.0 TB) does not match the files listed.
Investigation dates in PSI (2006-10-01 to 2022-05-31) span grant periods, not ISS operations (Nov 2017 to March 2021).
Coflow burner fuel-tube inner diameter: 2.1 mm in the 2014 NASA paper, 2.2 mm in the 2023 E-FIELD modelling preprint.
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions was found in the PSI files.

Publication review (data/publications/PSI-21.json): of the 18 listed publications (17 distinct), 3 were read in full via NTRS preprints (Cao 2015 counted twice, Ma 2015), 6 as abstracts, 9 not at all (Elsevier/Springer closed, no free abstract). Only Dobbins 2022 uses ACME CLD Flame ISS data; the rest are SLICE precursor or ground diagnostics and modelling work. No listed paper reports the CLD Flame dilution limits or lift-off heights; NASA cites the 2019 and 2021 US National Combustion Meeting papers (Tinajero et al.) for these, which remain unlocated.
